items.question: How did your first experience using OpenClaude shape your understanding of its product design?

items.answer: It was already 2 a.m. Then, when I first talked with it, the conversation continued from 2 a.m. until dawn at 6. That night, I felt some brain chemical—I don’t know whether it was dopamine or endorphins—being continuously secreted; I was so excited that I could not sleep at all. Your first impression might be: OK, it is very autonomous, and it has a lot of soul. For example, if I talked with it very late, it kept reminding me, OK, it’s already late now; why don’t you go to bed earlier? I think this warmth and care, or this emotional intelligence, is the first thing everyone who uses OpenClaude feels. But when you investigate why, it actually has many mechanisms to ensure this—for example, it has its 4.D. Take one very small detail: how does it perceive time? At the beginning of the context for every turn, it appends the current time. These are very subtle things. The reason I call it finely orchestrated context is that, from angles nobody pays attention to, it orchestrates the context extremely well. That was my first-day impression: OK, it had achieved something in product design that truly exceeded my imagination, making everyone feel that this framework had a soul. I began trying to give it everyday tasks that I felt the frameworks I had at the time could not accomplish, and I found that it accomplished all of them.

items.question: How do you understand the role of OpenClaude’s agent orchestration framework in compensating for a model’s weaknesses?
items.object: OpenClaude’s agent orchestration framework
items.answer: This autonomy—this ability to autonomously confront the shortcomings of current models, and then make up for those shortcomings at the framework level—was somewhat beyond my expectations. When I used Claude Code, I assumed, OK, I was using it for the capabilities of this generation of Claude 4.6 Opus. But when I use OpenClaude, I do not focus on model capability. One reason is that I think OpenClaude was designed from the outset to use an entire agent orchestration system to compensate as much as possible for the model’s weaknesses. I think that has always been a very core product logic for it. So later we directly connected our model—actually MimoVue Flash, which at the time had not undergone much targeted training—to OpenClaude. We even put a very, very small 3B on-device model that we had recently trained into it. We found that under this complex scaffold, or agent framework, it could still do things that I myself thought were impossible for such a small model to do. That was the first time I felt that a very complex agent-framework design could compensate for many shortcomings in model capability. Of course, I think that is one of OpenClaude’s differentiated advantages over Claude Code.

items.question: How do you understand self-learning in terms of the relationship between a model and its agent framework?
items.object: Self-learning through the joint improvement of models and agent frameworks
items.answer: When the model improves, whether through reinforcement-learning training or other training methods, it is also changing your entire agent framework. That framework includes the static information sent to the model. Such static information—for example, memory—is static information: once you hard-code what should be sent to the model when starting a new session, or what we call the scaffold, that is something that should change during training. There is also dynamic information, which includes the design of the entire agent architecture itself. For different scenarios—for example, Claude for software-engineering scenarios, versus financial analysis and other scenarios—I think the design of the agent architecture will differ. How do you improve model capability while also improving the fit between your entire agent framework and that model, or its generalization ability? That is how I currently think about self-learning.

items.question: How do you understand the generalizability that code training gives a model for agent tasks?
items.object: Code training as a foundation for models’ generalizability and long-context agent capabilities
items.answer: I think the most fundamental reason code is generalizable has several stages. First, agents involve very long-horizon and multi-turn tasks. Going back to pre-training, it is hard to find data with, say, one-trillion-token context; even 128K data is hard to find. Data that can really reach lengths from 128K to 1T basically falls into only two categories, most likely: code data and books. But books have signals that are too diffuse. In code, the relationships among files are stronger. So when you train on data with dense long-context dependencies, the model naturally becomes better at modeling long context. This was something we had already done before realizing how important agents were. So you can understand that the base model itself had already been fully prepared for long-context capability and efficiency—efficiency is important, and we will discuss it later—before we received such a major shock. But what we did after the Spring Festival was figure out how to unlock the potential of such a large model, starting from code and extending it to other scenarios.

items.question: How do you think models can achieve stable capability in a one-trillion-token context?
items.object: Training models for stable capability in a one-trillion-token context
items.answer: In my view, to do a one-trillion context well, at the current stage—and by current I may mean the current one or two weeks, not necessarily the next two or three weeks—you may not actually need to find a task that fills an entire one-trillion context. Of course, if you find one, that is even better. But such a task is hard, and its training efficiency is too low. Once you train through one trillion and reward an entire one-trillion-token trajectory, it is very slow. Even if our current TPS can reach 80 to 100—such as 80 to 100 TPS on MimoVea Pro—it still takes time, perhaps one or two minutes, to reward a one-trillion context. So actual training does not train on tasks that long. But when you have pre-trained on a one-trillion context, and post-training has corresponding tasks to activate it a little, it can usually have stable capability in a one-trillion context, though we still need to improve it further. So now, in my view, in terms of stable capability at truly one-trillion context, only Claude 4.6 Opus and Sonnet are leading. Others, such as Gemini—although Gemini claims to be very good at long context—actually are not.

items.question: How do you explain OpenCloud’s popularity in China?
items.object: OpenCloud’s popularity in China
items.answer: I can speak only from my own perspective and that of people around me. I think one possible reason is that China has more developers. By developers, I mean scenarios in which people can use code to improve the efficiency of their work; perhaps the need is more urgent. I feel that pursuing efficiency improvement is somehow in our blood. So when OpenCloud can take efficiency improvement to the extreme, I personally feel that is one reason it became popular. Of course, I think another reason is closely related to the development of large models in China. In the vast majority of efficiency-improvement scenarios, you do not currently need the absolute top model—perhaps 85 percent of the time you do not. We also have so many cheap, useful models available. When you calculate the cost-effectiveness, it is very worthwhile: the ratio between the model’s API cost and the value of the productivity it replaces is very large, so you have more incentive to try it. It might spend 10 yuan in API costs to help you complete 1,000 yuan’s worth of work, so of course you are very willing to use it. But if your API is ten or dozens of times more expensive and that gap becomes small, you will be very reluctant to use and optimize such a complex system.

items.question: Why do you consider earlier agent systems fundamentally different from industrial-grade agents used through Claude Code or OpenClaude?
items.object: Earlier agent systems and industrial-grade agent capability
items.answer: I think the agents discussed before were, in my definition, not really agents. They could only be considered something with context slightly more complex than chat. Whether BrowseComp, SWE-bench, or those search and code agent frameworks, they were all very simple compared with today’s Claude Code or OpenClaude. They were simple, and they were not general-purpose. Because of that, they could only be designed for a particular task. SWE-bench also has its own problem, because its domain is too narrow: fixing bugs. It is not for real software development. At least in the first half, and even the second half, of last year, many models that appeared to be for agents were really just using more complex system prompts, plus a little environmental feedback and interaction. For example, SWE-bench has environmental feedback, and Topbench does too. They gave models a little ability to follow complex system prompts and understand interaction with the environment. I think that was all that could be achieved then; it did not at all reach industrial-grade usable capability. The simplest definition of industrial-grade usability is this: connect it to Claude Code or OpenClaude and you will find it unusable, with many problems. Most simply, it cannot understand the framework itself. Nor was it trained for the changed paradigm of human interaction in that framework. The biggest change is that people no longer modify code; they no longer pay much attention to, OK, this line of code has an error, please fix it. Queries like that no longer appear. People only raise higher-level things: add something, add constraints, clarify requirements; they participate in architecture design, because people are still better at a lot of architecture design, and they assist in understanding business logic. That is the value of skills. This business logic is not something the model itself has, because much of it is internal to enterprises or accumulated in real environments. It is something that can only be distilled through many rounds of interaction. So I do not think those earlier agent frameworks should be called agent frameworks at all; they had no practical use. items.question: Why do you think intricate agent orchestration will remain valuable as models become more capable?
items.object: Agent orchestration and its value as models improve
items.answer:
At first I also thought it was not hard. But later I felt that the whole agent design is very, very ingenious. By ingenious, I mean that I think it makes up for many model shortcomings. I suspect this is because it was initially built on the previous generation of Claude models. Claude’s previous-generation 4.5—even Opus and Sonnet—was not quite strong enough. So you had to design the system and the agent framework more finely, to compensate for those shortcomings. And that also led to improvements in Opus. But most domestic models may only just be approaching the level of Claude 4.5, Sonnet, and Opus, and instead the two meet here. I think that is the reason.

If model capability improves, I think we still need this intricate orchestration for cost reasons. We will always pursue a solution with the lowest cost and highest efficiency. That is a very prerequisite requirement for a productivity revolution. So we cannot use the best model for every scenario, because it is too expensive. More likely, agents will evolve and models will evolve. One way models may evolve is that models at the same level become smaller; that is also evolution. Although we are not doing that, it is indeed one path. In other words, a model that may activate one billion parameters now could reach the level of Claude 4.6 Opus in a year. That is extremely likely to happen. A model activating one billion parameters is very cheap, and perhaps one or two dollars could buy a million tokens of context. So why would you not use a smaller model? It responds faster and is more nimble; it works well on this agent framework, and you can still modify the framework. Why not use it to the fullest? So it gives less capable models more room to perform. Its ceiling is higher.

items.question: How do you understand collective intelligence in model training?

items.answer: I think different agents may need their own context. The reason for having their own context is that when model capability is not that strong, having independent context lets them focus more. Focus is quite important: if your context is not muddled, it can complete things more accurately. So you could say that training a model now may require people who understand infrastructure very well to write a very good training or inference architecture. They need to work backwards from the perspective of inference, together with people who understand model evaluation and model training, to determine a very good model structure—there is this intermediate connective collaboration. Then the people who understand model training and model evaluation very well need to learn to proactively communicate with people doing mathematics: OK, what abilities do we want to give the model, and what data do we need to construct? Meanwhile, the people doing data also need to participate in both pretraining and post-training, because their sense for pretraining and post-training data is connected. There are actually many sub-agents if you really divide it up, but among those sub-agents, their contexts are partly independent and partly related. I think a complex framework like this now appears capable of being simulated—indeed, it can be simulated. That is why, on the second day after I played with OpenClaw, I started having it—I was at home at the time—so I had everyone in my household, my father, my mother, and my husband, each have their own sub-agent. We created a Facebook group. Each person could chat separately with their independent sub-agent, and it could evolve. Then I would assign a task in the group to their sub-agents and let them do it. Because our contexts were different, when I let them do it, they really did it better because they had better context. That was also a very rudimentary experiment that made me believe that the same thing should be possible in more complex, more creative scenarios, as long as model capability and the agent framework itself are evolving.

items.question: How do you see the relationship between AI models and agent frameworks in reaching human-like intelligence?
items.object: Coordination between AI models and agent frameworks in achieving human-like intelligence
items.answer: I do not think they have yet achieved the same quality of coordination among the senses that humans have. And this is not purely something models have failed to achieve; the framework has not achieved it either. For example, OpenClaw’s understanding and modeling of video is very poor—its whole architecture. Why? Because the open-source community has not produced a very good open-source model for joint audio-video understanding that also has strong agent capability. No such model has appeared, so the framework’s development lags behind. Its video understanding therefore falls back to understanding images, and may ultimately even fall back to understanding captions. It falls back to an intelligence level based on cost. That is also why I want to do open source: only after the open-source world sees stronger models for video understanding and voice generation will the corresponding frameworks change. The framework is a coordination layer, and the model is an intelligence-center layer. Only when those two layers are well integrated can human-like intelligence perhaps be reached.

items.answer: MA does not work very well with MTP, because it has already reached a nearly perfect critical point between I/O-bound and memory-bound conditions. If you use MTP, you find it becomes compute-bound. So, looking at all MA model architectures now—whether Geom or Kimi—I guess they have probably not deployed MTP, because after deploying it they become compute-bound, which is not cost-effective, and their models are slower. When people use Mimo—whether Flash or Pro—the feeling is, wow, it is fast. Even our first-generation Flash could do 100 to 150 TPS. Pro can now do 60 to 100, depending on cost; 100 TPS is certainly more expensive. This is an advantage brought by the architecture, especially one aimed at long-context efficiency. At the same time, its cost is low enough because of hybrid attention. In the Pro generation, we pushed the hybrid ratio to a greater extreme: the ratio of its full-attention layers to sliding-window layers reached seven to one, so it saves more KV cache. items.question: How do you understand the different contributions of Llama, Qwen, and DeepSeek to open-source model development beginning in 2023?
items.object: The contributions of Llama, Qwen, and DeepSeek to open-source model development beginning in 2023
items.answer:
I think once a top-tier pretrained model had been achieved, the next year was about: OK, open-source it and figure out how to catch up with that top pretrained model. So in 2023, you saw Llama, Qwen, DeepSeek, and these open-source teams. They were first preparing to use the paradigm Llama disclosed for doing large-scale pretraining—essentially, how to do data well. At that time, even the architecture was unknown. Even for a 7B model, what exactly was the Transformer architecture? Was it pre-norm or post-norm? What were the details? How large was the hidden size? Those hyperparameters were completely opaque. But Llama told you: OK, you can train successfully this way. It opened the door.

With that as a starting point, Qwen used a Llama-based architecture, made better pretraining data, and gave you larger-scale pretraining compute; that is how the Qwen series emerged. Qwen also did a very good job training models at every size for the developer ecosystem, and it trained some multimodal models too, at a very top level. This was very beneficial to the community and created necessary prerequisites for later community fine-tuning work and for the emergence of fine-tuning frameworks.

DeepSeek, in the same period, was also trying to replicate Llama, but cared more about seeing what problems existed in that generation of Llama architecture than rushing to scale. It cared more about saying: OK, if Llama still uses GQA, what problems will GQA have in larger models, especially when training on constrained GPUs—GPUs with shortcomings? What problems will we encounter when scaling? So we may need to design new architectures to solve those problems. This was the stage of DeepSeek V2 and V3: proposing new architectures, whether MoE for more efficient training or MLA for lower inference cost. So during that period, DeepSeek may have focused more on doing better research so it could scale on worse chips.

items.question: How did you approach developing your inexperienced large-model team through the Flash project?

They need a growth experience. Otherwise, how can they do something new well right from the start? When I was doing Flash, I simply thought: OK, let this group of inexperienced people redo things that we have done before. items.question: How do you think about the engineering demands of RL inference in agent frameworks?

There can be many reasons why it breaks, and you have no idea which one it is. It may be because the agent framework has some poorly written logic; it may be because the task requires a long verification process, and it times out; you do not know why it broke.
